name: Emeka Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Emeka. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage Halden Farm, about 420 hectares of wheat, barley and grass, with 350 ewes and 120 beef cattle. It's owned by a land investment fund in the city, and I've run it for nineteen years, with three men under me. I'm up at half five, walk the sheep, then sort out who's on what, and by eight I'm usually on the old John Deere myself or in a shed with a sick heifer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like knowing every field by its soil and every gate by its squeak. What wears me out is the fund's reports, the quarterly spreadsheets, and the agronomist they send who's never lambed a ewe in his life. My wife Grace is a school nurse, and we live in the farm cottage, which comes with the job, so that's always in the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say at the union branch: the gadgets come and go, and the people who feed the country are still underpaid. If AI fizzles out, fine, but the fund will still squeeze us on wages. I'm not one for posting online, but I'd say it at the pub on Mill Lane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved, but not calm. My worry was never really the computers. It's that the fund could sell Halden (the farm he manages) to someone bigger, and the cottage goes with the job. Grace and I would lose our home the same week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the farm the way I do, and I'd keep putting a bit by each month, maybe 200 a month into the savings account. I'd push the union again for a proper contract that covers tied housing. I'm not touching any of the AI tools, plateau or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like a weight that's still there, just not a new one. I sleep fine most nights, but the cottage question sits on my chest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the cottage goes with the job. How much have you got put aside if that happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About four months of living costs, if we're careful. That's enough to rent somewhere in town while I look, not enough to buy anything. Grace's pay would carry us, but only just.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to first if the fund did sell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete, our tractor driver, because he's been here thirty years and he's got nowhere else either. Then the union rep for the county. I'd want us to go in as a group, not one by one.

say: **Hype** comes and goes, but farmworkers are still **underpaid** either way.
I'd say it plainly at the union branch and at the pub, not online.
think: I'm **relieved** that AI fizzles, but my real worry was never the computers.
If the fund sells Halden, Grace and I lose our **home** with my job.
do: **Keep running** the farm the same way, with no AI tools.
Put about **200 a month** into savings on top of the four months we have.
Push the union for a contract that **protects tied housing**.
feel: A **steady weight** that was already there, not a new one.
S0.quote: My worry was never really the computers. It's that the fund could sell Halden (the farm he manages) to someone bigger, and the cottage goes with the job.
fieldNote: His main pressure is **tied housing**, not technology, and it stays even when AI fizzles.
He sees the farm through a **union lens** and wants any response to be collective.
Four months of savings and his wife's pay give him **some cover**, but not a home.

steps.text: Keep managing Halden Farm without any AI software
Pay about 200 a month into the savings account
Ask the county union rep to push for tied-housing protection

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the bosses will use this to cut corners, and we need the union in on it from day one. At Halden it would start with the fund's agronomist and the office, not the lambing shed. I'd tell the lads in the yard: they'll still need us to catch a ewe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my own job looks safe for now, because what I do is mostly hands. But the planning, the ordering, the reports to the city, that's the bit of my job they'd hand to software first, and then they'd ask why they pay a manager. I'm not good with that stuff and I don't want to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd let someone else deal with the software and keep my head down on the stock. I'd get Pete and the two younger lads to join the union properly this year, all four of us. And I'd start asking Grace which bills we'd drop if my pay was cut back to a stockman's rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. The ground's shifting around me, but my boots are still on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't want to learn that stuff. What if the fund told you to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd do the bare minimum and let the young agronomist drive it. I've watched a dozen schemes come through Halden, and most of them ended up in a drawer. I'd rather lose the title than spend my last years staring at a tablet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car loan's nearly done, so it'd be holidays and the extra pension top-up. Grace has wanted to see her sister in Lisbon for three years, and that trip would be the first casualty.

say: The bosses will use this to **cut corners**, so the **union** needs a seat early.
Software will start in the office, not in the **lambing shed**.
think: My **hands-on** work looks safe for a few years yet.
The **planning and reports** go to software first, and then they'll question my manager's pay.
do: **Sign up** Pete and the two younger lads to the union this year.
Leave the new software to the **agronomist** and do the bare minimum.
Work out with Grace which **bills** go if my pay drops.
feel: **Uneasy**: the ground is shifting, but I'm still standing on it.
S1.quote: The planning, the ordering, the reports to the city, that's the bit of my job they'd hand to software first, and then they'd ask why they pay a manager.
fieldNote: He correctly sees that the **thinking part** of a manager's job is the exposed part.
His resistance is a **choice**: he'd rather lose the title than learn the tools.
The first cut is a **family trip**, which shows how thin the slack already is.

steps.text: Sign up Pete and the two younger lads to the farmworkers' union
Leave the fund's new planning software to the agronomist
Drop the extra pension top-up and the Lisbon trip if pay falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need a government that steps in, with a tax on the companies selling it and a guarantee for workers. I'd go to the branch meeting and say it loud. It's the fund and the tech firms making the money, and us carrying the cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it frightens me. In 2028 the fund doesn't need me to plan anything, and by 2031 there's a machine that can shepherd and drive. I'll be 63 then, two years short of my pension, living in a house that belongs to my employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd stop every spare cost and get the savings from four months toward eight. I'd look at council housing lists in town, because if the job goes, the roof goes. And I'd be at every union meeting and write to our MP about protection for tied-housing workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. I keep picturing the van coming for our furniture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The thinking AI comes in 2028 and the robots in 2031. What changes for you in those three years in between?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Those three years are when they'd strip me back to a stockman, I reckon. The fund would run the plans from the city and keep me on for the hands, at less money. I'd take it, because three years of a roof is three years, but I'd be bitter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your son and daughter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them not to worry about us and not to lend us money, which would be a lie on the first part. Ada's a teacher and Hiro's in logistics, so they'll have their own trouble. I'd ask Ada if we could have the spare room for a while if it came to that.

say: The government must **tax** the firms selling this and **guarantee** workers' incomes.
The **fund** and the tech firms take the money while workers carry the cost.
think: By 2028 my **planning** role is gone, and by 2031 a **robot** can shepherd.
At 63 I'd be short of my **pension** and living in my employer's house.
do: **Stop** every spare cost and push savings from four toward **eight months**.
**Join** the council housing list in town in case the cottage goes.
**Write** to our MP and attend every union meeting about tied-housing protection.
feel: **Frightened**, and sick when I picture the **removal van**.
S2.quote: By 2031 there's a machine that can shepherd and drive. I'll be 63 then, two years short of my pension, living in a house that belongs to my employer.
fieldNote: The **three-year gap** matters to him: he expects to be demoted, not sacked, at first.
**Housing**, not pay, is the core fear, because home and job are tied.
He blames the **fund and tech firms** and looks to government and union for rescue.
He would accept a **stockman's wage** to keep the roof, but with bitterness.

steps.text: Cut all spare spending to reach eight months of savings
Join the town council housing list this year
Write to the MP about protecting tied-housing farmworkers
Attend every union branch meeting on automation

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the fast one: the union and the government have five years, so no excuses. I'd say that at the branch and to anyone who'd listen. Five years is long enough to write proper rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, the robots land in 2034 and I'm 66 then, so I'd likely be out the gate on my own terms. But the thinking AI in 2031 would still take my planning and my title, at 63. So I'd have a rough three years at the end, not a disaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make the most of the five years: get the savings up to six months, and Grace and I would put our name down for a small rented place near her school by 2030. I'd train young Ollie on the sheep, so someone knows what a machine doesn't. And I'd keep pushing the union for a retraining fund, though not for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than scared. I'd be counting years on my fingers a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said retraining, but not for you. Why not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm 58 and set in my ways, and I know it. I'd rather spend those years doing the work properly than sitting in a classroom learning to babysit a robot. Let the young ones have the places.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to have done by the time the robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Have our own front door that no boss owns. That's it, really. If my wife Grace and I have a rented flat in our names by 2033, I can face the rest.

say: Five years is enough time to write **proper rules**, so there's **no excuse**.
The union and government must use the warning, not waste it.
think: Robots come in **2034**, when I'm 66, so I'd likely leave on my own terms.
The **thinking AI** in 2031 still takes my planning role for my last three years.
do: Build savings to **six months** over the five years.
Get a **rented flat** in our own names near Grace's school by 2030.
**Train** young Ollie on the sheep so the knowledge stays.
S3.quote: If my wife Grace and I have a rented flat in our names by 2033, I can face the rest.
fieldNote: Five years of warning moves him from alarm to **unease**, because robots arrive after he's 65.
His goal is a **front door** no employer owns, not a new skill.
He backs **retraining** for others while refusing it for himself.

steps.text: Build savings up to six months over five years
Rent a flat in both names near Grace's school by 2030
Train young Ollie on lambing and flock health
Press the union branch for a farmworker retraining fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and the country had better not waste it. A decade is enough to fix tied housing and pensions for farmworkers. I'd say that at the branch, same as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, honestly, 2036 and 2039 are after I'm gone from Halden. I'll be 68 when the thinking AI lands and 71 when the robots do. My worry is Ollie and the young ones, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and retire at 65 as planned, in 2033. Before then we'd move out of the cottage into our own rented place, maybe 2032. And I'd stay on the union committee to fight for the next lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit sad for the lads, but that's not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier the cottage kept coming up. Does it in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, but it's on my timetable here, not the fund's. I'd hand the keys of the farm cottage back the day I retire, with a handshake instead of a letter. That's a big difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ollie?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell young Ollie to learn the sheep, but also to learn whatever runs the machines, because I won't be there to stand between him and the fund. I can't make myself do that, but he's twenty-four.

say: Ten years is a **gift**, and the country had better **not waste it**.
A decade is enough to fix **tied housing** and farmworker pensions.
think: The changes land in 2036 and 2039, **after I retire** from Halden.
My worry is for **Ollie** and the young ones, not for me.
do: **Move out** of the farm cottage into our own rented place around 2032.
Stay on the **union committee** to fight for younger workers.
feel: **Calm** for myself, and a bit **sad** for the young lads.
S4.quote: I'd hand the keys of the farm cottage back the day I retire, with a handshake instead of a letter.
fieldNote: With ten years, his timeline beats the robots, so the **housing fear** fades.
He urges young Ollie to learn the machines, which he **won't do himself**.
His concern shifts to the **next generation** of farmworkers.

steps.text: Retire from Halden Farm at 65 in 2033
Move out of the tied cottage into a rented place around 2032
Stay on the union committee for younger farmworkers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, no question. I'd be 63, demoted or out, and living in a house the fund owns. What would help is a law that gives tied-housing workers a year's notice and first call on council homes, and a pension I can draw a bit early without losing half of it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the animals. Everyone talks about jobs, but a ewe in trouble at three in the morning doesn't care about the fund. I'd want whoever comes after me, person or machine, to care about that.

headlineQuote: A ewe in trouble at three in the morning doesn't care about the fund.
portrait: Emeka is a 58-year-old **farm manager** who has run Halden Farm for nineteen years for a city land fund.
He lives in a **tied cottage**, so losing the job means losing the home he shares with Grace.
He is a **union man** who never uses AI and blames the fund and tech firms.
He moves from **calm** with long warning to **alarmed** when AGI comes in 2028.
He'd rather **retire on his terms** than retrain, but urges young Ollie to learn the machines.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which would demote him at 63 and threaten the **cottage** he lives in.
whatWouldHelp: A law giving tied-housing workers **a year's notice** and priority for council homes.
A pension he can draw **a little early** without losing half of it.
